label: def:2.1
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:2.1}\cite{douglas1998}
	Let $T$ be an operator on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$.
	If the range of $T$ is finite‑dimensional, then $T$ is called a
	\textit{finite‑rank operator}.
	If $T$ maps the unit ball of $\mathcal{H}$ into a compact set, then $T$ is called a \textit{compact operator}.
	Denote by $\mathfrak{F}(\mathcal{H})$ and $\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{H})$ the sets of all finite‑rank operators and compact operators on $\mathcal{H}$, respectively.

label: def:2.2
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:2.2}\cite{douglas1998}
	Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a Hilbert space. The quotient algebra $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})/\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{H})$ is called the \textit{Calkin algebra}.
	Let $\pi$ denote the canonical homomorphism from $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ onto $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})/\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{H})$.
	For $T\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$, the spectrum of $\pi(T)$ in the Calkin algebra is called the \textit{essential spectrum} of $T$, denoted by $\sigma_e(T)$.

title: Theorem

\label{thm:2.4}\cite{douglas1998}
	Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a Hilbert space. An operator $T\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ is Fredholm if and only if $\operatorname{ran}T$ is closed, and both $\ker T$ and $\ker T^*$ are finite‑dimensional.

\label{def:2.9}
	Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a Hilbert space and let $\{\xi_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ and $\{\eta_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be two sequences of vectors in $\mathcal{H}$. We call $\{\xi_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ and $\{\eta_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ \textit{biorthogonal sequences} if
	\[
	\langle\xi_m,\eta_n\rangle=\delta_{m,n},\quad \forall\,m,n\in\mathbb{N}.
	\]
	If furthermore, $\operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{\xi_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}=\operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{\eta_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}=\mathcal{H}$, we call $\{\xi_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ and $\{\eta_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ \textit{dual systems}.

label: def:2.10
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:2.10}\cite{wells2008differential}
	Let $E\to \Omega$ be a vector bundle. A \textit{Hermitian metric} $h$ on $E$ assigns to each fibre $E_x$ of $E$ a Hermitian inner product $\langle{\cdot,\cdot}\rangle_x$, such that for any open subset $U\subset\Omega$ and any $\xi,\eta\in \mathcal{E}(U,E)$, the function
	\[
	\langle\xi,\eta\rangle\colon U\to \mathbb{C}
	\]
	defined by
	\[
	\langle\xi,\eta\rangle(x)=\langle\xi(x),\eta(x)\rangle_x
	\]
	is of class $C^\infty$.

label: def:2.11
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:2.11}\cite{wells2008differential}
	Let $E\to\Omega$ be a vector bundle. A \textit{connection} $D$ on $E\to\Omega$ is a $\mathbb{C}$‑linear map
	\[
	D\colon \mathcal{E}(\Omega,E)\to \mathcal{E}^1(\Omega,E),
	\]
	satisfying
\[
		D(\varphi\xi)=d\varphi\cdot\xi+\varphi D\xi,
		\label{eq:connection-leibniz}
\]
	where $\varphi\in\mathcal{E}(\Omega)$ and $\xi\in\mathcal{E}(\Omega,E)$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
\cite{wells2008differential}
	Let $D$ be a connection on the vector bundle $E\to\Omega$. The \textit{curvature} $\Theta_E(D)$ is defined to be the element
	\[
	\Theta\in\mathcal{E}^2\bigl(\Omega,\operatorname{Hom}(E,E)\bigr),
	\]
	the $\mathbb{C}$‑linear map
	\[
	\Theta\colon \mathcal{E}(\Omega,E)\to\mathcal{E}^2(\Omega,E),
	\]
	which has the local representation with respect to a frame
	\[
	\Theta(f)=\Theta(D,f)=d\theta(f)+\theta(f)\wedge\theta(f).
	\]

title: Definition
body_md:
\cite{wells2008differential}
	For an $\mathcal{S}$‑bundle $E\xrightarrow{\pi}\Omega$, an $\mathcal{S}$‑\textit{section} is an $\mathcal{S}$‑morphism $s\colon \Omega\to E$ satisfying
	\[
	\pi\circ s=\mathbf{1}_\Omega,
	\]
	where $\mathbf{1}_\Omega$ denotes the identity mapping on $\Omega$. That is, $s$ maps each point of the base space into the fibre over that point.

label: keni
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{keni}\cite{fang2026invariantII}
	Let \(T \in B(\mathcal{H} \oplus \mathcal{H})\) be an invertible conjugate bi-geometric operator given by
	\[
	T = \begin{bmatrix}
		A & T_{12} \\
		0 & B
	\end{bmatrix}.
	\]
	Choose nonzero vectors \(e_0 \in \ker A^*\) and \(f_0 \in \ker B\) such that \(\langle T_{12}f_0, e_0 \rangle = 1\). Let \(A_L^{-1}\) be the unique left inverse of \(A\) such that \(A A_L^{-1} = I - T_{12}f_0 \otimes e_0\); and \(B_R^{-1}\) be the unique right inverse of \(B\) such that \(B_R^{-1}B = I - f_0 \otimes T_{12}^*e_0\). Then
	\[
	T^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
		A_L^{-1} & -A_L^{-1}T_{12}B_R^{-1} \\
		f_0 \otimes e_0 & B_R^{-1}
	\end{bmatrix}.
	\]

label: defin1
title: Definition
body_md:
(bundle-preserving operator)\label{defin1}
	Let
	\[
	T=\begin{pmatrix}
		A & T_{12}\\
		0 & B
	\end{pmatrix}\in \mathcal{B}(M\oplus M^\perp),
	\]
	where $A^{*},B\in B_1(O_\delta)$. If there exists some $\alpha\in(0,+\infty)$ such that $T_{12}e_B(\lambda)=e_{A_{L,\alpha}^{-1}}(\lambda)$ for all $\lambda\in O_\delta$, then \(T\) is said to have \textit{bundle-preserving property}; equivalently, \(T\) is called a \textit{bundle-preserving operator}.

label: lem:3.4
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:3.4}
	Suppose $A_L^{-1}A = I$, $e_0'\in\ker A_L^{-1}$ and $e_0\in\ker A^*$. Then $\langle e_0',e_0\rangle\neq 0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that $\langle e'_0, e_0 \rangle = 0$. Since
$e_0 \in \ker A^*, \  A^* \in B_1(O_\delta),$
	it follows that $e'_0 \perp \ker A^*$, hence $e'_0 \in \overline{\operatorname{ran} A}$. As $A$ is Fredholm, its range is closed, so $e'_0 \in \operatorname{ran} A.$

	Thus, there exists a nonzero $x$ such that $Ax = e'_0$. It implies that
	\[
	A_L^{-1}Ax = A_L^{-1}e'_0 = 0.
	\]
	 	Then $x=0$, contradicting the choice of $x\neq0$. Therefore the assumption is false, and  $\langle e'_0, e_0 \rangle \neq 0$.

label: lem:3.5
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let
$
x \in \bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty} \operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{A^n e_0' : n \ge k\}.
$
Then for each $k \in \mathbb{N}$, we have
\[
x \in \operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{A^n e_0' : n \ge k\}.
\]
Since $A^n e_0' \in \operatorname{\overline{ran}} A^k$ whenever $n \ge k$, it follows that
$
x \in \operatorname{\overline{ran}} A^k.
$
As $A$ is Fredholm, $\operatorname{ran} A^k$ is closed, so $x \in \operatorname{ran} A^k$. Thus
\[
x \in \bigcap_{n=0}^{\infty} \operatorname{ran} A^n.
\]
Since $A^* \in B_1(O_\delta)$, it is well known that
$
\bigcap_{n=0}^{\infty} \operatorname{ran} A^n = \{0\}.
$
Consequently,
\[
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty} \operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{A^n e_0' : n \ge k\} = \{0\}.
\]
	
	

	
For each $k \in \mathbb{N}$, set
\[
\mathcal H_k := \overline{\operatorname{Span}}\{A^n e_0' : n \ge k\}.
\]
Assume that $\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty} \mathcal H_k = \{0\}$. We claim that the sequence $\mathcal H_k$ is strictly decreasing, i.e.
\[
\mathcal H_0 \supsetneq \mathcal H_1 \supsetneq \mathcal H_2 \supsetneq \cdots .
\]
Suppose, there exists some $k$ such that $\mathcal H_k = \mathcal H_{k+1}$. Since $A^k e_0' \in \mathcal H_k = \mathcal H_{k+1}$, we have
\[
A^{k+1} e_0' = A(A^k e_0') \in A(\mathcal H_{k+1}) \subset \mathcal H_{k+2}.
\]
As $\mathcal H_{k+1}$ is generated by $\{A^{k+1} e_0', A^{k+2} e_0', \ldots\}$, and $A^{k+1} e_0' \in \mathcal H_{k+2}$, it follows that
$
\mathcal H_{k+1} = \mathcal H_{k+2}.
$
 Repeating the same argument inductively yields
\[
\mathcal H_k = \mathcal H_{k+1} = \mathcal H_{k+2} = \cdots .
\]
Consequently, $\bigcap_{j=0}^{\infty} \mathcal H_j = \mathcal H_k$, which is contradicting the assumption. Hence $\mathcal H_0 \supsetneq \mathcal H_1 \supsetneq \mathcal H_2 \supsetneq \cdots$.
	
	We now prove that for any $N\in\mathbb{N}$,
	\[
	\mathcal{H}=\operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{A^k e_0': 0\le k\le N\}\dot{+}\mathcal{H}_{N+1}.
	\]
	First, we show $\operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{A^{n}e_{0}^{\prime}: 0\le n\le N\}\cap \mathcal{H}_{N+1}=\{0\}$.
	Suppose $w\in \operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{A^{n}e_{0}^{\prime}: 0 \le n\le N\}$ and $v\in \mathcal{H}_{N+1}$ satisfy $w=v$. If $w\neq 0$, then $w=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\alpha_iA^{i}e_{0}^{\prime}=v$. We may assume that $\alpha_j=-1$ and $\alpha_i=0$ for $1\le i<j$. Then
	\[
	A^{j}e_{0}^{\prime}=\sum_{i=j+1}^{N}\alpha_iA^{i}e_{0}^{\prime}+v\in \mathcal{H}_{j+1}.
	\]
	This implies that $\mathcal{H}_j=\mathcal{H}_{j+1}$. This contradicts $\mathcal{H}_0\supsetneq \mathcal{H}_1\supsetneq \mathcal{H}_2\supsetneq\cdots$.
	
	Second, we show for every $x\in \mathcal{H}$, there is $y\in \operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{A^{n}e_{0}^{\prime}: 0 \le n\le N\}$ and $z\in \mathcal{H}_{N+1}$ such that $x=y+z$. Note that there exists a sequence of vectors $\{x_n\}$ in $\mathcal{H}$ such that each $x_n$ can be written as a finite linear combinations of $\{A^{n}e_{0}^{\prime}\}$ and $\lim_{n\to\infty}\|x_n-x\|=0$. In particular, there is $y_n\in \operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{A^{n}e_{0}^{\prime}: 0 \le n\le N\}$ and $z_n\in \mathcal{H}_{N+1}$ such that $x_n=y_n+z_n$. Let $\pi$ be the quotient map from $\mathcal{H}$ onto $\mathcal{H}/\mathcal{H}_{N+1}$.
	
	Then $\pi(y_n)=\pi(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal{H}/\mathcal{H}_{N+1}$. Clearly, $\pi$ is a surjective map from $\operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{A^{n}e_{0}^{\prime}: 0 \le n\le N\}$ onto $\operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{\pi(A^{n}e_{0}^{\prime}): 0 \le n\le N\}$. Suppose $\pi(w_0e_{0}^{\prime}+w_1 Ae_{0}^{\prime} +\cdots+w_NA^{N}e_{0}^{\prime})=0$. Then there exists a $v\in \mathcal{H}_{N+1}$ such that $w_0e_{0}^{\prime}+w_1 Ae_{0}^{\prime} +\cdots+w_NA^{N}e_{0}^{\prime}=v$. Thus $w_0e_{0}^{\prime}+w_1 Ae_{0}^{\prime} +\cdots+w_NA^{N}e_{0}^{\prime}=v=0$. So $\pi$ is an injective map from $\operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{A^{n}e_{0}^{\prime}: 0 \le n\le N\}$ onto $\operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{\pi(A^{n}e_{0}^{\prime}): 0 \le n\le N\}$.
	
	Since $\operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{A^{n}e_{0}^{\prime}: 0\le n\le N\}$ is finite dimensional, $\{y_n\}$ is a Cauchy sequence. Thus $\{z_n\}$ is also a Cauchy sequence. Let $y=\lim_{n\to\infty} y_n$ and $z=\lim_{n\to\infty} z_n$. Then $y\in \operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{A^{n}e_{0}^{\prime}: 0\le n\le N\}$ and $z\in \mathcal{H}_{N+1}$ such that $x=y+z$. This implies $\mathcal{H}=\operatorname{\overline{Span}}\{A^{n}e_{0}^{\prime}: 0\le n\le N\}\dotplus \mathcal{H}_{N+1}$.
	
	Set $N=0$. Then
$
	\mathcal H = \operatorname{Span}\{e_0'\} \dot{+}\mathcal H_1
$
	holds. Define the operator
	\[
	P : \mathcal H \to \operatorname{Span}\{e_0'\},
	\]
	by $P(x) = c e_0'$ whenever $x = c e_0' + x_1$ with $x_1 \in \mathcal H_1$. It is clear that $P$ is a bounded idempotent. Now define a linear functional
	\[
	f : \mathcal H \to \mathbb C,
	\]
	by the condition $P(x) = f(x) e_0'$. This definition is well-posed, and $f$ is obviously linear. Since
	\[
	\|f(x) e_0'\| = \|P(x)\| \le M \|x\| \quad (M := \|P\|),
	\]
	we have
$
	|f(x)| \le \frac{M}{\|e_0'\|} \|x\|,
$
hence $f \in \mathcal H^*$. By the Riesz representation theorem, there exists $g_0 \in \mathcal H$ such that
	\[
	f(y) = \langle y, g_0 \rangle \quad (y \in \mathcal H).
	\]
	Consequently,
	\[
	\langle e_0', g_0 \rangle = 1,\qquad \langle A^n e_0', g_0 \rangle = 0 \quad (n \ge 1).
	\]
	
	
	For $N=1$, the same argument yields a bounded idempotent
	\[
	Q : \mathcal H \to \operatorname{Span}\{e_0', Ae_0'\},
	\]
	and a linear functional
	\[
	\phi : \operatorname{Span}\{e_0', Ae_0'\} \to \mathbb C,
	\]
	such that
	\[
	\phi(e_0') = 0,\qquad \phi(Ae_0') = 1.
	\]
	Since the projection $P_1 : \operatorname{Span}\{e_0', Ae_0'\} \to \overline{\operatorname{Span}}\{e_0'\}$ is bounded, it follows that for any $c_0, c_1 \in \mathbb C$,
	\[
	|\phi(c_0 e_0' + c_1 Ae_0')|
	= |c_1|
	= \frac{\|c_1 Ae_0'\|}{\|Ae_0'\|}
	\le \frac{\|P_1\|}{\|Ae_0'\|} \cdot \|c_0 e_0' + c_1 Ae_0'\|.
	\]
	
	
Hence $\phi \circ Q \in \mathcal H^*$, and it satisfies
$
(\phi \circ Q)(A^n e_0') = 0 \  (n \neq 1),\
(\phi \circ Q)(A e_0') = 1.
$
By the Riesz representation theorem, there exists $g_1 \in \mathcal H$ such that
\[
\langle A^n e_0', g_1 \rangle = 0 \quad (n \neq 1),\qquad
\langle A e_0', g_1 \rangle = 1.
\]
Repeating the above argument, we obtain a sequence $\{g_n\}_{n=0}^{\infty} \subset \mathcal H$ such that
\[
\langle A^m e_0', g_n \rangle = \delta_{mn} \quad (m,n \ge 0).
\]

label: thm:3.7
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:3.7}
Let $T$ be a conjugate bi-geometric operator in $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$. If $T$ has the bundle-preserving property, then $T^{-1}$ is intransitive.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $T$ is a conjugate bi-geometric operator,
it can be represented as
	\[
	T=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		A & T_{12}\\
		0 & B
	\end{pmatrix}\in \mathcal{B}(M\oplus M^{\perp}),
	\]
	where $A^{*},B\in B_1(O_\delta)$.
	
	 Since $A^{*},B\in B_1(O_\delta)$, we have
	\[
	\bigcap_{n=0}^{\infty}\operatorname{ran}A^{n}=\{0\},\quad
	\bigcap_{n=0}^{\infty}\operatorname{ran}(B^{*})^{n}=\{0\}.
	\]
Since $T$ has the bundle-preserving property, there exists $\alpha\in(0,+\infty)$ such that
	\[
	T_{12}e_{B}(\lambda)=e_{A_{L,\alpha}^{-1}}(\lambda).
	\]
Differentiating both sides n times yields:
\[
\begin{cases}
	T_{12}e_B^{(1)}(\lambda) = e_{A_{L,\alpha}}^{(1)}(\lambda) \\
	T_{12}e_B^{(2)}(\lambda) = e_{A_{L,\alpha}}^{(2)}(\lambda) \\
	\vdots \\
	T_{12}e_B^{(n)}(\lambda) = e_{A_{L,\alpha}}^{(n)}(\lambda)
\end{cases}.
\]
	Furthermore, evaluating the $n$-th derivative of $e_B$ at $\lambda=0$ gives:
	\[
	\begin{cases}
		e_B^{(1)}(0) = B_R^{-1}f_0 \\
		e_B^{(2)}(0) = 2!(B_R^{-1})^2f_0 \\
		\vdots \\
		e_B^{(n)}(0) = n!(B_R^{-1})^nf_0
	\end{cases}.
	\]
	Similarly,
\[
\begin{cases}
	e_{A_{L,\alpha}}^{(1)}(0) = \alpha A e_0' \\
	e_{A_{L,\alpha}}^{(2)}(0) = 2! \alpha^2 A^2 e_0' \\
	\vdots \\
	e_{A_{L,\alpha}}^{(n)}(0) = n! \alpha^n A^n e_0'
\end{cases}.
\]
	Therefore, $T_{12}\big(e_B^{(n)}(0)\big)=e_{A_{L,\alpha}^{-1}}^{(n)}(0)$, i.e.
	\[
	T_{12}(B_R^{-1})^n f_0=\alpha^n A^n e_0'.
	\]
	We may assume $\langle e_0,e_0'\rangle=1$ by Lemma \ref{lem:3.4}. Since $e_0\in\ker A^*$, we obtain
	\[
	\langle A^n e_0',e_0\rangle=\langle e_0,(A^*)^n e_0\rangle=0,\quad n\ge 1.
	\]
	Then
	\[
	A_L^{-1}T_{12}(B_R^{-1})(B_R^{-1})^n f_0=\alpha^{n+1}A^n e_0'.
	\]
	
A direct computation shows that
	\[
	T^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}e_0'\\0\end{pmatrix}
	=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		A_L^{-1} & -A_L^{-1}T_{12}(B_R^{-1})\\
		f_0\otimes e_0 & (B_R^{-1})
	\end{pmatrix}
	\begin{pmatrix}e_0'\\0\end{pmatrix}
	=
	\begin{pmatrix}0\\f_0\end{pmatrix},
	\]
	
	\[
	T^{-2}\begin{pmatrix}e_0'\\0\end{pmatrix}
	=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		A_L^{-1} & -A_L^{-1}T_{12}(B_R^{-1})\\
		f_0\otimes e_0 & (B_R^{-1})
	\end{pmatrix}
	\begin{pmatrix}0\\f_0\end{pmatrix}
	=
	\begin{pmatrix}-\alpha e_0'\\(B_R^{-1})f_0\end{pmatrix},
	\]
	
	\[
	T^{-3}\begin{pmatrix}e_0'\\0\end{pmatrix}
	=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		A_L^{-1} & -A_L^{-1}T_{12}(B_R^{-1})\\
		f_0\otimes e_0 & (B_R^{-1})
	\end{pmatrix}
	\begin{pmatrix}-\alpha e_0'\\(B_R^{-1})f_0\end{pmatrix}
	=
	\begin{pmatrix}-\alpha^2 A e_0'\\-\alpha f_0+(B_R^{-1})^2 f_0\end{pmatrix},
	\]
	

	Claim that for $k\ge 3$,
	\[
	T^{-k}\begin{pmatrix}e_0'\\0\end{pmatrix}
	=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		-\alpha^{k-1}A^{k-2}e_0'\\
		-\alpha(B_R^{-1})^{k-3}f_0+(B_R^{-1})^{k-1}f_0
	\end{pmatrix}. \tag{1}\label{123}
	\]
	Suppose that the (\ref{123}) holds for $k=n$,
	then
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		T^{-(n+1)}\begin{pmatrix}e_0'\\0\end{pmatrix}
		&=
		\begin{pmatrix}
			A_L^{-1} & -A_L^{-1}T_{12}(B_R^{-1})\\
			f_0\otimes e_0 & (B_R^{-1})
		\end{pmatrix}
		\begin{pmatrix}
			-\alpha^{n-1}A^{n-2}e_0'\\
			-\alpha(B_R^{-1})^{n-3}f_0+(B_R^{-1})^{n-1}f_0
		\end{pmatrix}\\[10pt]
		&=
		\begin{pmatrix}
			-\alpha^{n}A^{n-1}e_0'\\
			-\alpha(B_R^{-1})^{n-2}f_0+(B_R^{-1})^{n}f_0
		\end{pmatrix}.
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	Thus, (\ref{123}) holds for $k=n+1$.
	Hence, (\ref{123}) holds for all $k\ge 3$. By Lemma \ref{lem:3.5}, there exists a sequence $\{g_n\}_{n=0}^{\infty} \subset M$ such that
	\[
	\langle A^n e_0', g_m \rangle = \delta_{n,m} \quad \text{for all } n,m \ge 0.
	\]
	Hence	\[
	\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\langle T^{-k}e_0^{\prime},g_0\rangle z^k=1-\alpha z^2.
	\]
	By Lemma \ref{lem:3.6}, taking $f=e_0^{\prime}, g=g_{0}$ and $v(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\langle T^{-n}f,g\rangle=1-\alpha z^2$, we conclude that $T^{-1}$ is intransitive.

label: collo3.6
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{collo3.6}
		Let
		\[
		T = \begin{pmatrix} A & T_{12} \\ 0 & B \end{pmatrix}
		\]
		be an invertible conjugate bi-geometric operator. If there exists an operator
	$Y \in \operatorname{ran} \tau_{A,B}$
	such that
		\[
		\begin{pmatrix} A & Y + T_{12} \\ 0 & B \end{pmatrix}
		\]
		has the bundle-preserving property, then $T^{-1}$ intransitive.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Without loss of generality, let $Y = AX - XB$, set $G = \begin{pmatrix} I & -X \\ 0 & I \end{pmatrix}$, clearly $G^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} I & X \\ 0 & I \end{pmatrix}$. Then
			\[
			GTG^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} I & -X \\ 0 & I \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} A & T_{12} \\ 0 & B \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} I & X \\ 0 & I \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A & Y + T_{12} \\ 0 & B \end{pmatrix}.
			\]
			By Theorem \ref{thm:3.7}, $GTG^{-1}$ satisfies the third problem of Halmos. Hence $T^{-1}$ is intransitive.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let
		\[
		T = \begin{pmatrix} S & T_{12} \\ 0 & S^* \end{pmatrix},
		\]
		where $T_{12}$ is defined on $H^2$ by
		\[
		T_{12}x = \langle x, e_0 \rangle e_0 + \langle x, e_1 \rangle e_1 + a_1 \langle x, e_1 \rangle e_2 + \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \langle x, e_n \rangle \bigl( e_n + a_n e_{n+1} - a_{n-1} e_{n-1} \bigr)
		\]
		for $x \in H^2$, with $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} |a_n|^2 < \infty$ and $a_N \neq 0$ for some $N \in \mathbb Z^+$. It follows that $T_{12}\in B(H^{2})$.
		
		Let
		\[
		H = \begin{pmatrix} S^* & -S^* T_{12} S \\ e_0 \otimes e_0 & S \end{pmatrix},
		\]
		then $HT = TH = I$ and hence $T$ is invertible.
		
		Furthermore,
		\[
		T_{12} e_N = e_N + a_N e_{N+1} - a_{N-1} e_{N-1} \neq \alpha e_N
		\]
		for any scalar $\alpha$. Consequently, $T$ does not have the bundle-preserving property.
		
		
		Let
		\[
		X = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n} e_n \otimes e_n,
		\]
		and set $Y = SX - XS^*\in ran\tau_{S,S^{*}}$, then \[\begin{cases}
			(T_{12}-Y)e_{0}=e_{0}\\
			(T_{12}-Y)e_{1}=e_{1}+a_{1}e_{2}-a_{1}e_{2}=e_{1}\\
			(T_{12}-Y)e_{n}=e_{n}+a_{n}e_{n+1}-a_{n-1}e_{n-1}-(a_{n}e_{n+1}-a_{n-1}e_{n-1})=e_{n},\  n\ge 2.
		\end{cases}\]
		Hence, $T_{12}+(-Y) = I$. Consequently, the operator
		\[\tilde{T}=
		\begin{pmatrix} S & T_{12} +(-Y) \\ 0 & S^* \end{pmatrix}
		\]
		have the bundle-preserving property. By Corollary \ref{collo3.6}, $T^{-1}$ is intransitive.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{dingli00}
			Let
			\[
			T=\begin{pmatrix}A & T_{12}\\0 & B\end{pmatrix}
			\]
			be a conjugate bi-geometric operator with \(\sigma(T)=\mathbb{T}\), and
			\[
			T^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}
				A_L^{-1}&-A_L^{-1}T_{12}B_R^{-1}\\
				f_0\otimes e_0&B_R^{-1}
			\end{pmatrix}.
			\]where \(f_{0},e_{0}\) satisfy \(\langle T_{12}f_{0},e_{0}\rangle=1\).
			If
			\[
			\|A^n\|,\|B^n\|,\|(A_L^{-1})^n\|,\|(B_R^{-1})^n\|
			=O(e^{an^\alpha}),\qquad  n\in \mathbb{N}_{0},
			\]
			where \(\alpha \in (0,1), a>0\), then \(T^{-1}\) is intransitive. In particular, \(T^{-1}\) possesses a nontrivial hyperinvariant subspace.

label: yinli1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{yinli1}
			Let
			\[
			T=\begin{pmatrix}
				A&T_{12}\\
				0&B
			\end{pmatrix}.
			\]
			If \(\max\{\|A^{n}\|,\|B^{n}\|\}=O(e^{an^{\alpha}}), n\in \mathbb N_0
			\), where \(\alpha \in (0,1), a>0\), then \(\|T^{n}\|=O(e^{an^{\alpha}}), n\in \mathbb N_0
			\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For \(n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}\), it is clear that
			\[
			T^n=\begin{pmatrix}
				A^n & \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}A^j T_{12}B^{n-j-1}\\
				0 & B^n
			\end{pmatrix}.
			\]
			Then there exist constants \(C_1,C_2>0\) such that
			\[
			\begin{aligned}
				\|T^n\|
				&\le C_1 e^{an^\alpha}+C_2 e^{an^\alpha}
				+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\|A^j\|\|T_{12}\|\|B^{n-j-1}\|\\
				&\le C_1 e^{an^\alpha}+C_2 e^{an^\alpha}
				+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}C_1 e^{aj^\alpha}\|T_{12}\|C_2 e^{a(n-j-1)^\alpha}\\
				&\le (C_1+C_2)e^{an^\alpha}
				+nC_1C_2\|T_{12}\|e^{2a(n-1)^\alpha}.
			\end{aligned}
			\]
			And there exists a constant \(C_3>0\) such that
			\[
			ne^{2a(n-1)^\alpha}\le C_3 e^{an^\alpha}.
			\]
			Hence
			\[
			\|T^n\|\le (C_1+C_2+C_1C_2C_3\|T_{12}\|)e^{an^\alpha},\qquad n\in \mathbb N_0
			.
			\]
head: environment

label: yinli2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{yinli2}
			Let
			\[
			W=\begin{pmatrix}A & T_{12}\\0 & B\end{pmatrix}
			\]
			be a bounded operator such that
			\[
			\|W^n\| =O(e^{an^\alpha}),n\in \mathbb N_0
			,
			\]where $ 0<\alpha<1,\ a>0$.
			If there exists a rank-one operator \(F\) such that
			\(T=\begin{pmatrix}
				A&T_{12}\\
				F&B
			\end{pmatrix}\) is invertible and
			\(\sigma(T)\subset\mathbb{T}\), then there exist \(\beta\in(0,1),\ b>0\) such that
			\[
			\|T^n\|=O(e^{bn^{\beta}}), n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}.
			\]

title: Proof
body_md:
Obviously,
			\[
			(I-zT)^{-1}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} z^n T^n,
			\]
			By the Cauchy integral formula, for \(r\in(0,1)\), we have
			\[
			T^n=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|z|=r}\frac{(I-zT)^{-1}}{z^{n+1}}dz, \qquad n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}.
			\]
			Hence
			\[
			\|T^n\|\le r^{-n}\sup_{|z|=r}\|(I-zT)^{-1}\|, \qquad n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}.
			\]
			Hence, we are reduced to estimating \(\|(I-zT)^{-1}\|\).
			From \(\|W^n\|\le Ce^{an^\alpha}, \ C>0\), we get \(r(W)\le1\). Thus for all \(0<|z|<1\), we have \(\left|\frac1z\right|>1\) and \(\frac1z\in\rho(W)\). Hence
			\[
			I-zW=-z\left(W-\frac1z I\right).
			\]
			Since \(W-\frac1z I\) is invertible, \((I-zW)\) is invertible.
			
			\textbf{Step 1}: Compute \((I-zT)^{-1}\).
			Let
			\[
			R(z)=(I-zW)^{-1}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty z^k W^k.
			\]
			Let \(F=f_{0}\otimes e_{0}\), take \(u=(0,f_0)\), \(v=(e_0,0)\), and set \(N=u\otimes v\), then \(T=W+N\).
			Let
			\[
			d(z)=1-z\langle R(z)u,v\rangle,\qquad z\in\mathbb D.
			\]
			Clearly,
			\[
			|d(z)|\le1+|z|\|N\|\|R(z)\|.
			\]
			Since \(\sigma(T)\subset \mathbb T\), we claim that \(d(z)\) has no zeros on \(\mathbb D\).
			
			If there exists \(z_0\in\mathbb D\) such that \(d(z_0)=0\), let \(x=R(z_0)u\). Then
			\[
			(I-z_0W)x=u\ne0,
			\]
			so
			\[
			\begin{aligned}
				(I-z_0T)x&=(I-z_0W-z_0N)R(z_0)u\\
				&=u-z_0NR(z_0)u\\
				&=u-z_0\langle R(z_0)u,v\rangle u\\
				&=\big(1-z_0\langle R(z_0)u,v\rangle\big)u\\
				&=d(z_0)u\\
				&=0.
			\end{aligned}
			\]
			Thus \(I-z_0T\) is not invertible, which contradicts \(\sigma(T)\subset\mathbb T\). Hence \(d\) has no zeros in \(\mathbb D\).
			
			Since
			\[
			\begin{aligned}
				(I-zT)R(z)u&=(I-zW-zN)R(z)u\\
				&=(I-zW)R(z)u-z\langle R(z)u,v\rangle u\\
				&=u-z\langle R(z)u,v\rangle u\\
				&=d(z)u.
			\end{aligned}
			\]
			Let
			\[
			X=R(z)+\frac{z}{d(z)}R(z)NR(z).
			\]
			Because
			\[
			\begin{aligned}
				NR(z)NX&=NR(z)\langle X,v\rangle u\\
				&=\langle X,v\rangle NR(z)u\\
				&=\langle X,v\rangle\langle R(z)u,v\rangle u\\
				&=a(z)NX,
			\end{aligned}
			\]where $a(z)=\langle R(z)u,v\rangle$.
			we have
			\[
			1-za(z)=d(z),
			\]
			and
			\[
			NR(z)N=a(z)N.
			\]
			Thus
			\[
			\begin{aligned}
				(I-zT)X
				&=(I-zW-zN)\left(R(z)+\frac{z}{d(z)}R(z)NR(z)\right)\\
				&=I+\frac{z}{d(z)}NR(z)-zNR(z)-\frac{z^2}{d(z)}NR(z)NR(z).
			\end{aligned}
			\]
			Since \(NR(z)NR(z)=a(z)NR(z)\), we get
			\[
			\begin{aligned}
				(I-zT)X
				&=I+\left(\frac{z}{d(z)}-z-\frac{z^2a(z)}{d(z)}\right)NR(z)\\
				&=I+\left(\frac{z(1-za(z))}{d(z)}-z\right)NR(z)\\
				&=I+\left(\frac{zd(z)}{d(z)}-z\right)NR(z)\\
				&=I.
			\end{aligned}
			\]
			Similarly, \(X(I-zT)=I\). Hence \((I-zT)^{-1}=X\). Therefore
			\[
			\|(I-zT)^{-1}\|\le\|R(z)\|+\frac{\|N\|}{|d(z)|}\|R(z)\|^2.
			\]
			\textbf{Step 2}: Estimate \(\dfrac{1}{|d(z)|}\) and \(\|R(z)\|\).
			
			\textbf{First}, we estimate \(\sup_{|z|\le r}\|R(z)\|\).
			
			Let
			\[
			p=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}>0,
			\]
			and let \(\delta=1-r\). Clearly there exists a constant \(C_{\alpha}>0\) such that
			\(k^{\alpha}-\dfrac{\delta}{2a}k\le C_{\alpha}\delta^{-p}\).
			
			Since
			\[
			\|R(z)\|\le \sum_{k=0}^\infty \|W^k\|\cdot|z|^k
			\le C\sum_{k=0}^\infty e^{ak^\alpha} r^k,\qquad |z|\le r,
			\]
			and \(r=1-\delta\le e^{-\delta}\), so \(r^k\le e^{-k\delta}\). we have
			\[
			\|R(z)\|\le \sum_{k=0}^\infty Ce^{ak^\alpha-k\delta}
			\le \sum_{k=0}^\infty Ce^{aC_\alpha \delta^{-p}-\frac{\delta k}{2}}
			=\sum_{k=0}^\infty C e^{aC_\alpha\delta^{-p}} e^{-\frac{\delta k}{2}}
			=C e^{aC_\alpha\delta^{-p}} \frac{1}{1-e^{-\frac{\delta}{2}}}
			\le \frac{4C}{\delta}e^{aC_\alpha\delta^{-p}}.
			\]
			Let \(t=\frac1\delta>1\). Then	$\frac1\delta\le e^{\frac1p\delta^{-p}}.$
		
			Therefore
			\[
			\|R(z)\|\le 4C e^{\left(\frac1p+aC_\alpha\right)\delta^{-p}},
			\qquad \delta=1-r,\ |z|\le r.
			\]
			So
			\[
			\sup_{|z|\le r}\|R(z)\| \le M_1 e^{M_2\delta^{-p}},
			\qquad M_1=4C,\ M_2=\frac1p+aC_\alpha.\tag{4.1}\label{1.1.1}
			\]
			
			\textbf{Second}, we estimate \(|\dfrac{1}{d(z)}|\).
			
			From (\ref{1.1.1}), we obtain
			\[
			|d(z)|\le (1+\|N\|M_{1})e^{M_{2}(1-r)^{-p}}\le e^{K_{2}(1-r)^{-p}},
			\]
			where \(K_{2}>0\) is a constant, and \(d(0)=1\). Let \(h(z)=\log|d(z)|\). Then \(h(0)=0\), and
			\[
			\frac{1}{|d(z)|}=e^{-h(z)}.
			\]
			Take \(s=\frac{1+r}{2}\), and let
			\[
			M=\frac{K_2+1}{(1-s)^p}.
			\]
			Thus
			\[
			h(z)\le K_2(1-r)^{-p}\le \frac{K_2+1}{(1-s)^p},\qquad z\in B(0,r).
			\]
			Therefore \(u(z)=M-h(z), z\in B(0,s)\) is positive and harmonic. By Harnack's inequality, we have
			\[
			M-h(z)\le \frac{s+r}{s-r}M.
			\]
			So
			\[
			-h(z)\le \frac{s+r}{s-r}M-M=\frac{2rM}{s-r}.
			\]
			Since
			\[
			s-r=\frac{1-r}{2},\qquad 1-s=\frac{1-r}{2},
			\]
			we obtain
			\[
			-h(z)\le \frac{4}{1-r}\cdot\frac{2^p(K_2+1)}{(1-r)^p}
			=\frac{K_3}{(1-r)^{p+1}},
			\]
			where
			$
			K_3=4\cdot2^p(K_2+1)
			$
			is a fixed constant. Therefore
			\[
			\sup_{|z|\le r}\frac{1}{|d(z)|}\le e^{\frac{K_3}{(1-r)^{p+1}}}.
			\]
			Thus
			\[
			\|(I-zT)^{-1}\|\le M_1 e^{M_2(1-r)^{-p}}
			+\frac{\|N\|}{|d(z)|}M_1^2 e^{2M_2(1-r)^{-p}}.\tag{4.2}\label{1.1.2}
			\]
			\textbf{Step 3}: Estimate \(\sup_{|z|\le r}\|(I-zT)^{-1}\|\) and \(\|T^n\|, n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}\).
			
			From (\ref{1.1.2}), we get
			\[
			\sup_{|z|\le r}\|(I-zT)^{-1}\|
			\le M_1 e^{M_2(1-r)^{-p}}
			+\|N\|e^{\frac{K_3}{(1-r)^{p+1}}}M_1^2 e^{2M_2(1-r)^{-p}}.
			\]
			Since
			\[
			\frac{1}{(1-r)^{p+1}}\ge\frac{1}{(1-r)^p},
			\]
			we have
			\[
			\sup_{|z|\le r}\|(I-zT)^{-1}\|
			\le M_1 e^{M_2(1-r)^{-(p+1)}}
			+\|N\|M_1^2 e^{(K_3+2M_2)(1-r)^{-(p+1)}}
			\le M_3 e^{M_4(1-r)^{-(p+1)}},
			\]
			where
			\[
			M_3=M_1+\|N\|M_1^2,\qquad
			M_4=M_2+K_3+2M_2.
			\]
			Therefore
			\[
			\|T^n\|\le r^{-n}\cdot M_3 e^{M_4(1-r)^{-(p+1)}},
			\qquad \text{for all }0<r<1, \qquad n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}.
			\]
			Let
			\[
			q=p+1=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}.
			\]
			For \(n\ge1\), take
			\[
			\delta_n=\frac12 n^{-\frac1{q+1}},\qquad r_n=1-\delta_n\in(0,1).
			\]
			It is well known that
			\[
			-\log(1-\delta_n)\le2\delta_n.
			\]
			Therefore
			\[
			r_n^{-n}=e^{-n\log r_n}
			=e^{n(-\log(1-\delta_n))}
			\le e^{2n\delta_n}=e^{n^{\frac{q}{q+1}}},
			\]
			and
			\[
			\frac{1}{(1-r_n)^q}=\delta_n^{-q}
			=2^q n^{\frac{q}{q+1}}.
			\]
			Thus
			\[
			\|T^n\|
			\le e^{n^{\frac{q}{q+1}}} M_3 e^{M_4 2^q n^{\frac{q}{q+1}}}
			=M_3 e^{(1+M_42^q)n^{\frac{q}{q+1}}}
			=M_3 e^{M_5 n^{\frac{q}{q+1}}},\qquad n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}.
			\]
			where \( M_5=1+M_42^q.\)
			Moreover,
			\[
			\frac{q}{q+1}
			=\frac{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}}{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}+1}
			=\frac{1}{2-\alpha}\in(0,1).
			\]
			Hence \(\|T^{n}\|=O(e^{M_{5} n^{\beta}}),n\in \mathbb{N}_{0},\ \  \beta\in (0,1)\). This completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{yinli1}, it is easy to see that
			\[
			\|T^n\|\le C e^{an^\alpha},\qquad n\in \mathbb{N}_{0},
			\]
			where \(C>0\) is a constant.
			Obviously,
			\[
			T^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}
				A_L^{-1} & -A_L^{-1}T_{12}B_R^{-1}\\
				f_0\otimes e_0 & B_R^{-1}
			\end{pmatrix}=W+Q,
			\]
			where
			\[
			W=\begin{pmatrix}
				A_L^{-1} & -A_L^{-1}T_{12}B_R^{-1}\\
				0 & B_R^{-1}
			\end{pmatrix},\qquad
			Q=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\f_0\otimes e_0 & 0\end{pmatrix}.
			\]
			Similarly, \(\|W^n\|=O(e^{an^\alpha}), n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}\). Since \(W+Q=T^{-1}\) is essentially unitary and
			\[
			\sigma(T^{-1})\subset\mathbb T,
			\]
			by Lemma \ref{yinli2}, we have
			\[
			\|T^{-n}\|=O(e^{M n^\beta}),\qquad
			\beta=\frac{1}{2-\alpha}\in(0,1),\qquad n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}.
			\]
			where \(M\) is a constant.
			Hence there exist \(\gamma\in(0,1)\) and \(C_2>0\), with \(\gamma>\alpha\) and \(\gamma>\beta\), such that
			\[
			\|T^n\|=O(e^{C_2|n|^\gamma}),\qquad n\in\mathbb Z.
			\]
			Consequently,
			\[
			\|T^n\|\le C_1 e^{C_2 |n|^{\gamma}},\qquad C_{1}>0 \qquad n\in \mathbb{Z}.
			\]
				Choose a positive integer \(N\) such that
			\[
			\frac{N}{N+1}>\gamma.
			\]
			Set
			\[
			\theta=\frac{N}{N+1}>\gamma,\qquad s=1+\frac1N,
			\]
			then \(\theta<1\), and \(\theta=\frac1s\). Let
			\[
			\eta(t)=
			\begin{cases}
				e^{-(1-t^2)^{-N}}, & |t|<1,\\[2mm]
				0, & |t|\ge1.
			\end{cases}
			\]
			\textbf{Step 1}. Prove that there exists a constant \(B>0\) such that
			\[
			\|\eta^{(j)}\|_\infty\le B^j (j!)^s,\qquad j\ge0.
			\]
			
			Fix \(|t|<1\), and set \(v=1-t^2>0\). Take
			$
			\varepsilon=\frac{1}{24N}.
			$
			For \(|z-t|\le \varepsilon v\), set
			$
			\xi=\frac{t^2-z^2}{v},
			$
			then
			$
			1-z^2=v(1+\xi).
			$
			Moreover,
			\[
			|\xi|
			\le \frac{|z-t||z+t|}{v}
			\le \varepsilon v\frac{|z+t|}{v}
			=\varepsilon |z+t|
			\le \varepsilon(2|t|+\varepsilon v)
			\le 3\varepsilon
			=\frac1{8N}.
			\]
			Clearly,
			\[
			|\log(1+\xi)|
			\le \sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{|\xi|^m}{m}
			\le \frac{|\xi|}{1-|\xi|}.
			\]
			Thus
			\[
			|N\log(1+\xi)|
			\le \frac{N|\xi|}{1-|\xi|}
			\le N\dfrac{1}{8N-1}=\dfrac{1}{8-\frac{1}{N}}
			\le \frac17.
			\]
			It is well known that
			\[
			|e^w-1|\le e^{|w|}-1.
			\]
			Take \(w=N\log(1+\xi)\). Then
			\[
			\left|(1+\xi)^{-N}-1\right|
			=\left|e^{-N\log(1+\xi)}-1\right|
			\le e^{|N\log(1+\xi)|}-1
			\le e^{\frac{1}{7}}-1
			\le \frac12.
			\]
			And
			\[
			\operatorname{Re}(1+\xi)^{-N}
			=1+\operatorname{Re}\big((1+\xi)^{-N}-1\big)
			\ge 1-\left|(1+\xi)^{-N}-1\right|
			\ge \frac12.
			\]
			Since \(1-z^2=v(1+\xi)\), we have
			\[
			\operatorname{Re}(1-z^2)^{-N}\ge \frac12 v^{-N}.
			\]
			Hence
			\[
			\left|e^{-(1-z^2)^{-N}}\right|
			=e^{-\operatorname{Re}(1-z^2)^{-N}}
			\le e^{-\frac12 v^{-N}}.
			\]
			Let
			\[
			F(z)=e^{-\frac{1}{(1-z^2)^N}},\qquad z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{1,-1\}.
			\]
			Let \(\rho=\varepsilon v\). Since
			\[
			\rho=\varepsilon(1-t^2)
			=\varepsilon(1-|t|)(1+|t|)
			\le 2\varepsilon(1-|t|)
			<1-|t|,
			\]
			and
			\[
			\min\{|t-1|,|t+1|\}=1-|t|,
			\]
			we have \(z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{1,-1\}\) when \(|z-t|<\varepsilon v\). By Cauchy's integral formula, we get
			\[
			\eta^{(j)}(t)=F^{(j)}(t)
			=\frac{j!}{2\pi i}\int_{|z-t|=\varepsilon v}
			\frac{F(z)}{(z-t)^{j+1}}\,dz.
			\]
			Therefore
			\[
			|\eta^{(j)}(t)|
			\le \frac{j!}{2\pi}
			\frac{e^{-\frac12 v^{-N}}}{(\varepsilon v)^{j+1}}
			\cdot 2\pi(\varepsilon v)
			= j!\,(\varepsilon v)^{-j}e^{\frac{-v^{-N}}{2}}.
			\]
			Let \(x=v^{-N}\). Then
			\[
			|\eta^{(j)}(t)|
			\le j!\,\varepsilon^{-j}x^{\frac{j}{N}}e^{\frac{-x}{2}}.
			\]
			Maximizing \(x^{\frac{j}{N}}e^{\frac{-x}{2}}\) gives
			\[
			\sup_{x>0}x^{\frac{j}{N}}e^{\frac{-x}{2}}
			=\left(\frac{2j}{eN}\right)^{\frac{j}{N}}.
			\]
			Since \(j!\ge (\dfrac{j}{e})^j\), we obtain
			\[
			|\eta^{(j)}(t)|
			\le \big[\varepsilon^{-1}(\dfrac{2}{N})^{\frac{1}{N}}\big]^j (j!)^{1+\frac{1}{N}}.
			\]
			And \(|\eta(t)|\le1\). Take
			\[
			B=\max\{1,\varepsilon^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{N}\right)^{\frac{1}{N}}\},
			\]
			which yields the assertion.
			
			For fixed \(j\), as \(t\to\pm1\), \(v\to0\), and
			\[
			v^{-j}e^{\frac{-v^{-N}}{2}}\xrightarrow{v\to 0}0.
			\]
			Thus \(\eta\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)\).
			
			\textbf{Step 2}. Construct nonzero functions \(\varphi\ and \ \psi\).
			
			Take two distinct points in \(\sigma(T)\), denoted by \(e^{i\lambda_1},e^{i\lambda_2}\), and set
			\[
			d_0=|\lambda_1-\lambda_2|.
			\]
			Set \(d=\frac14d_0\), let
			\[
			\varphi(e^{it})=\eta\left(\frac{t-\lambda_1}{d}\right),\qquad
			\psi(e^{it})=\eta\left(\frac{t-\lambda_2}{d}\right),\qquad t\in[0,2\pi].
			\]
			Clearly,
			\[
			\operatorname{supp}\varphi
			\subset\left[\lambda_1-\frac14d_0,\lambda_1+\frac14d_0\right],
			\]
			\[
			\operatorname{supp}\psi
			\subset\left[\lambda_2-\frac14d_0,\lambda_2+\frac14d_0\right].
			\]
			Thus
			\[
			\varphi\psi=0,
			\]
			and
			\[
			\varphi(\lambda_1)=\psi(\lambda_2)=1\ne0.
			\]
			Moreover,
			\[
			|\varphi^{(j)}(t)|
			=\left|\frac{\eta^{(j)}\big(\frac{t-\lambda_1}{d}\big)}{d^j}\right|
			\le \frac{\|\eta^{(j)}\|_\infty}{d^j}
			\le \left(\frac{B}{d}\right)^j (j!)^s
			=B_0^j (j!)^s,
			\]
			where
			$
			B_0=\frac{B}{d}.
			$
			Obviously, \(\varphi,\psi\) are bounded on \(\mathbb T\), so \(\varphi,\psi\in L^2(\mathbb T)\). Let
			\[
			a_k=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\varphi(e^{it})e^{-ikt}\,dt,\qquad
			b_k=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\psi(e^{it})e^{-ikt}\,dt.
			\]
			For \(k\ne0\), integrating by parts \(j\) times gives
			\[
			|a_k|
			\le \frac{1}{2\pi |k|^j}\int_0^{2\pi}|\varphi^{(j)}(t)|\,dt
			\le \frac{\|\varphi^{(j)}\|_\infty}{|k|^j}
			\le \frac{B_0^j(j!)^s}{|k|^j}
			\le \left(\frac{B_0 j^s}{|k|}\right)^j.
			\]
			Let
			$
			x=\left(\frac{|k|}{2B_0}\right)^{1/s}.
			$
			When \(x\ge1\), take \(j=[ x]\ge1\). Then
			\[
			\frac{B_0 j^s}{|k|}
			\le \frac{B_0\left(\big(\frac{|k|}{2B_0}\big)^{\frac{1}{s}}\right)^s}{|k|}
			=\frac12.
			\]
			Hence
			\[
			|a_k|\le 2^{-j}\le 2e^{-(\log 2)x}.
			\]
			When \(x<1\), i.e. \(\frac{|k|}{2B_0}<1\), there are only finitely many such \(k\). Therefore we may assume
			\[
			|a_k|\le 2e^{-b x}
			=2e^{-b\left(\frac{|k|}{2B_0}\right)^{\frac{1}{s}}}
			=2e^{-c_1|k|^\theta},
			\]
			where
			\[
			\theta=\frac1s<1,\qquad b=\log2,\qquad
			c_1=\frac{b}{(2B_0)^{\frac{1}{s}}}.
			\]
			Similarly,
			\[
			|b_k|\le 2e^{-c_2|k|^\theta},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.
			\]where \(c_2>0\) is a constant.
			Thus
			\[
			|a_k|+|b_k|\le 4e^{-c|k|^\theta},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,
			\]
			where \(c=\max\{c_1,c_2\}\). Consequently,
			\[
			\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}(|a_k|+|b_k|)<+\infty.
			\]
			Let
			\[
			F(e^{it})=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k e^{ikt},\qquad t\in [0,2\pi].
			\]
			Then
			\[
			|F(e^{it})|\le \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|a_k|<+\infty,
			\]
			so \(\sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}}a_k e^{ikt}\) converges absolutely and uniformly, hence
			\[
			F(e^{it})\in L^2(\mathbb T),
			\]
			and
			\[
			\hat F(k)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}F(e^{it})e^{-ikt}\,dt=a_{k}=\widehat{\varphi}(k),\qquad k\in \mathbb{Z}.
			\]
			Thus \(F=\varphi\), i.e.
			\[
			\varphi(e^{it})=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\hat\varphi(k)e^{ikt}\in L^2(\mathbb T),
			\]
			and the series converges absolutely and uniformly. Similarly,
			\[
			\psi(e^{it})=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}b_k e^{ikt}\in L^2(\mathbb T),
			\]
			and it converges absolutely and uniformly.
			
			\textbf{Step 3}. Construct nonzero operator \(U,V\).
			Let
			\[
			U=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k T^k,\qquad
			V=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}b_k T^k.
			\]
			Since
			\[
			\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\|a_kT^k\|
			\le \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}2e^{-c|k|^\theta}\|T^k\|
			\le C_1\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}
			2e^{-c|k|^\theta+C_2|k|^\gamma},
			\]
			and \(\theta>\gamma\), there exists \(N_0\) such that for \(|k|\ge N_0\),
			\[
			C_2|k|^\gamma\le \frac c2|k|^\theta.
			\]
			Hence,
			\[
			\sum_{|k|\ge N_0}
			e^{-c|k|^\theta+C_2|k|^\gamma}
			\le \sum_{|k|\ge N_0}
			e^{-\frac c2|k|^\theta}<+\infty.
			\]
			Therefore \(\sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} a_kT^k\) and \(\sum_{k\in \mathbb{Z}} b_kT^k\) both converge, so \(U,V\) are well-defined.
			
			Since,
			\[
			\sum_{j,k\in\mathbb Z}|a_jb_k|\|T^{j+k}\|
			\le
			\left(\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|a_j|\|T^j\|\right)
			\left(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|b_k|\|T^k\|\right)
			<+\infty,
			\]
			we have
			\[
			UV=VU
			=\sum_{l\in\mathbb Z}
			\left(\sum_{j+k=l}a_jb_{l-j}\right)T^l.
			\]
			Note that
			\[
			\varphi(t)\psi(t)
			=\sum_{j,k\in\mathbb Z}a_jb_k e^{i(j+k)t},
			\]
			hence
			\[
			\widehat{(\varphi\psi)}(l)
			=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}a_jb_{l-j}.
			\]
			Since \(\varphi\psi=0\), we have \(\widehat{(\varphi\psi)}(l)=0\), and therefore
			\[
			UV=VU=0.
			\]
			Let
			\[
			\mathcal A=
			\left\{
			f:\ f(e^{it})=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_n e^{int},\quad
			\|f\|_{\mathcal A}
			=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}|a_n|\|T^n\|<+\infty
			\right\}.
			\]
			If \(f,g\in\mathcal A\), then
			\[
			(fg)(e^{it})=\sum_{n,m\in \mathbb{Z}}a_nb_m e^{i(n+m)t}
			=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}
			\left(\sum_{m+n=k}a_nb_m\right)e^{ikt}.
			\]
			Since,
			\[
			\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}
			\left|\sum_{m+n=k}a_nb_m\right|\|T^k\|
			\le
			\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\sum_{m+n=k}|a_nb_m|\|T^k\|
			\le
			\left(\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}|b_m|\|T^m\|\right)
			\left(\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}|a_n|\|T^n\|\right)
			<+\infty.
			\]
			Thus
			\[
			\|fg\|_{\mathcal A}\le \|f\|_{\mathcal A}\|g\|_{\mathcal A},
			\]
			so \(fg\in\mathcal A\). It follows that \(\mathcal A\) is a Banach algebra.
			
			Define
			\[
			\Phi:\mathcal A\to B(H),\qquad
			\Phi(f)=f(T)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_nT^n.
			\]
			Then it implies that $\|\Phi\|\le 1$ and
			\[
			\Phi(fg)
			=\sum_{n,m}a_nb_m T^{m+n}
			=f(T)g(T)
			=\Phi(f)\Phi(g).
			\]
			For \(f(e^{it})=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_n e^{int}\in\mathcal A\), set
			\[
			P_N(e^{it})=\sum_{n=-N}^N a_n e^{int}.
			\]
			For \(N=1,2,\dots\), take a trigonometric polynomial \(q_N(e^{it})\) such that
			\[
			P_N(e^{it})-P_N(\lambda)
			=(e^{it}-\lambda)q_N(e^{it}),
			\]
			then
			\[
			\lim_{N\to\infty}(e^{it}-\lambda)q_N(e^{it})
			=f(e^{it})-f(\lambda)
			\]
			converges in \(\mathcal A\) in norm. Consequently,
			\[
			(T-\lambda I)q_N(T)\to f(T)-f(\lambda)I
			\quad\text{in the operator norm as }N\to\infty.
			\]
			Since \(\lambda\in\sigma(T)\), \(T-\lambda I\) is not invertible. Hence for each \(N\), \((T-\lambda I)q_N(T)\) is not invertible. Since the set of non-invertible elements is closed, the limit \(f(T)-f(\lambda)I\) is also not invertible, i.e.,
			$
			f(\lambda)\in\sigma(f(T)).
			$
			Finally, Since \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are not identically zero on \(\sigma(T)\), it follows that \(U\) and \(V\) are nonzero.
		Hence there exist \(u,v\) such that \(Uu\neq 0\) and \(Vv\neq 0\). Consequently,
		\[
		\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\langle T^{-n}Uu,Vv\rangle z^{n}
		=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\langle T^{-n}VUu,v\rangle z^{n}=0
		\]
		is a rational function. Therefore, by Lemma \ref{lem:3.6}, \(T^{-1}\) is intransitive.
		In view of the definitions of \(U\) and \(V\), for \(B\in\{T^{-1}\}'=\{T\}'\), we have \(BU=UB\). Hence \(\overline{\operatorname{ran}U}\) is a nontrivial invariant subspace of \(B\). Consequently, \(T^{-1}\) possesses a nontrivial hyperinvariant subspace.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{mingttiiiB1}
			Let \(T=\begin{pmatrix}A & T_{12}\\0 & B\end{pmatrix}\), and \(\langle T_{12}f_0,e_0\rangle=1\). Let \(A^*,B\in B_1(O_{\delta})\). Let \(L,R\) be the standard left inverse and standard right inverse of \(A,B\), respectively, and
			\[
			\max\{\|A^n\|,\|B^n\|,\|L^n\|,\|R^n\|\}\le Me^{an^\delta}, \ n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}
			\]
			where \(M,a>0\), \(\delta\in(0,1)\). Let
			\[
			C=L-LT_{12}f_0\otimes e_0,\qquad D=R-f_0\otimes R^*T_{12}^*e_0.
			\]
			Then there exist constants \(A_{1}, A_{2}>0\) and \(\gamma\in (0,1)\) such that
			\[
			\|C^{n}\|,\|D^{n}\|\le A_{1}e^{A_{2}n^{\gamma}}, n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}
			\]
			if and only if
			\[
			h_A(z)=\langle(I-zL)^{-1}T_{12}f_0,e_0\rangle,\qquad
			h_B(z)=\langle T_{12}(I-zR)^{-1}f_0,e_0\rangle
			\]
			are zero free on \(\mathbb{D}\).

title: Proof
body_md:
By the Cauchy integral formula,
			\[
			\|C^{n}\|\le r^{-n}\sup_{|z|\le r}\|(I-zC)^{-1}\|,n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}, \qquad \forall\,0<r<1.
			\]
			Therefore, to estimate \(\|C^{n}\|\), we first need to estimate \(\sup_{|z|\le r}\|(I-zC)^{-1}\|\), and hence first compute \((I-zC)^{-1}\).
			
			\textbf{Step 1}, compute \((I-zC)^{-1}\).
			
			Let
			\[
			e(z)=(I-\overline zL^*)^{-1}e_0,\qquad f(z)=(I-\overline zR)^{-1}f_0.
			\]
			Then
			\[
			A^*e(z)=A^*(I-\overline zL^*)^{-1}e_0
			=A^*\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\overline z^n(L^*)^ne_0
			=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\overline z^n(L^*)^{n-1}e_0
			=\overline z\,e(z).
			\]
			Similarly, \(Bf(z)=zf(z)\). Hence
			\[
			\ker(A^*-\overline z I)=\operatorname{span}\{e(z)\},\qquad
			\ker(B-z I)=\operatorname{span}\{f(z)\}.
			\]
			Let
			\[
			u=T_{12}f_0,\qquad v=T_{12}^{*}e_0.
			\]
			Then
			\[
			C=L-Lu\otimes e_0,\qquad D=R-f_0\otimes R^*v.
			\]
			Let
			\[
			F_L(z)=(I-zL)^{-1},\qquad F_R(z)=(I-zR)^{-1},\qquad P=Lu\otimes e_0,\qquad Q=f_0\otimes R^*v,
			\]
			and
			\[
			F_L(z)=(I-zL)^{-1}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}z^nL^n
			=I+z\left(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}z^nL^n\right)L=I+zF_L(z)L.
			\]
			Thus
			\[
			\begin{aligned}
				1+z\langle F_L(z)Lu,e_0\rangle
				&=\langle T_{12}f_0,e_0\rangle+z\left\langle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}z^nL^{n+1}u,e_0\right\rangle\\
				&=\langle T_{12}f_0,e_0\rangle+\left\langle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}z^{n+1}L^{n+1}T_{12}f_0,e_0\right\rangle\\
				&=\left\langle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}z^nL^nT_{12}f_0,e_0\right\rangle\\
				&=\langle(I-zL)^{-1}T_{12}f_0,e_0\rangle\\
				&=h_A(z).
			\end{aligned}
			\]
			Similarly,
			\[
			h_B(z)=1+z\langle F_R(z)f_0,R^*v\rangle.
			\]
			Let \(k(z)=F_L(z)P\). Then
			\[
			k(z)x=F_L(z)Px=F_L(z)\langle x,e_0\rangle Lu.
			\]
			Hence
			\[
			\begin{aligned}
				k(z)^{2}x
				&=\langle k(z)x,e_0\rangle F_{L}(z)Lu\\
				&=\langle\langle x,e_0\rangle F_L(z)Lu,e_0\rangle F_L(z)Lu\\
				&=\langle x,e_0\rangle\langle F_L(z)Lu,e_0\rangle F_L(z)Lu\\
				&=a(z)\,k(z)x,
			\end{aligned}
			\]
			where \(a(z)=\langle F_L(z)Lu,e_0\rangle.\)
			Thus \(k(z)^2=a(z)\,k(z)\).
			
			We have
			\[
			(I+zk(z))\left(I-\frac{z}{h_A(z)}k(z)\right)
			=\left(I+\left(z-\frac{z}{h_A(z)}-\frac{z^{2}a}{h_A(z)}\right)k(z)\right)=I,
			\]
			and similarly
			\[
			\left(I-\frac{z}{h_A(z)}k(z)\right)(I+zk(z))=I.
			\]
			Since
			\[
			I-zC=I-zL+zP=(I-zL)\bigl(I+zF_L(z)P\bigr).
			\]
			we get
			\[
			(I-zC)\left(I-\frac{z}{h_A(z)}k(z)\right)F_L(z)=I,
			\]
			and similarly
			\[
			\left(I-\frac{z}{h_A(z)}k(z)\right)F_L(z)(I-zC)=I.
			\]
			Therefore
			\[
			(I-zC)^{-1}=\left(I-\frac{z}{h_A(z)}k(z)\right)F_L(z).
			\]
			
			\textbf{Step 2}, Estimate \(\dfrac{1}{|h_A(z)|}, \|k(z)\|,\|F_{L}(z)\|\).
			
			Clearly,
			\[
			\|F_L(z)\|\le\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|z|^n\|L^n\|\le\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}Me^{an^\delta}r^n,\qquad |z|\le r.
			\]
			It is known that there exists a constant \(C_{1}>0\) such that
			\[
			an^\delta\le\frac{t}{2}n+C_{1}t^{-p},\qquad n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}
			\]where $p=\dfrac{\delta}{1-\delta}$.
			And
			\[
			r^n=(1-t)^n=e^{n\log(1-t)}\le e^{-tn},\  n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}.
			\]
			Hence
			\[
			\sup_{|z|\le r}\|F_L(z)\|
			\le Me^{C_{1}t^{-p}}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{-\frac{tn}{2}}
			=Me^{C_{1}t^{-p}}\frac{1}{1-e^{-\frac{t}{2}}}
			\le\frac{4}{t}Me^{C_{1}t^{-p}}.
			\]
			Since
		$
			\frac{1}{t}=e^{\log\frac{1}{t}}\le e^{pt^{-p}},
		$
			we obtain
			$
			\sup_{|z|\le r}\|F_L(z)\|\le M_1e^{K_1t^{-p}},
		$
			where \(M_1,K_1\) are constants. Consequently,
			\[
			\sup_{|z|\le r}\|k(z)\|\le \|P\|M_{1}e^{K_{1}t^{-p}}.
			\]
			Similarly
			\[
			|h_A(z)|\le\|F_L(z)\|\|T_{12}\|\|f_0\|\|e_0\|\le M_2e^{K_1(1-r)^{-p}},\qquad |z|\le r,
			\]where $M_{2}=M_{1}\|T_{12}\|\|f_{0}\|\|e_{0}\|.$
			Let \(U(z)=\log|h_A(z)|\), \(U(0)=0\). Then
			\[
			U(z)\le\log M_2+\frac{K_1}{(1-r)^p}.
			\]
			Let
			\[
			M_R=\log M_2+\frac{K_1}{(1-R)^p},\qquad R=\frac{1+r}{2},
			\]
			then \(M_R-U(z)\) is positive and harmonic. By Harnack's inequality, we obtain
			\[
			M_R-U(z)\le\frac{R+r}{R-r}M_R.
			\]
			Hence
			\begin{align*}
				-U(z)
				&\le\frac{2r}{R-r}M_R\\
				&=\frac{2r}{R-r}\left(\log M_2+\frac{K_1}{(1-R)^p}\right)\\
				&	=\frac{4r}{1-r}\left(\log M_2+\frac{2^pK_1}{(1-r)^p}\right)\\
				&	\le\frac{4}{1-r}\left(\log M_2+\frac{2^pK_1}{(1-r)^p}\right)\\
				&\le \dfrac{C_{2}}{(1-r)^{p+1}}, \qquad |z|\le r
			\end{align*}
		where \(C_2=4(\log M_{2}+2^{p}K_{1})\) is independent of \(r\). Therefore
			\[
			\sup_{|z|\le r}\frac{1}{|h_A(z)|}\le\sup_{|z|\le r}e^{-U(z)}\le e^{\frac{C_2}{(1-r)^{p+1}}}.
			\]
			Thus
	\begin{align*}
		\|(I-zC)^{-1}\|
			&\le\left(1+\frac{|z|}{|h_A(z)|}\|k(z)\|\right)\|F_L(z)\|\\
		&\le\left(1+e^{\frac{C_2}{(1-r)^{p+1}}}M_{1}\|P\|e^{K_{1}(1-r)^{-p}}\right)M_{1}e^{K_1(1-r)^{-p}}\\
	&	\le (1+M_{1}\|P\|)e^{\frac{C_{2}+2K_{1}}{(1-r)^{p+1}}}\\
&	=K_{2}e^{\frac{K_{3}}{(1-r)^{p+1}}},.
			\end{align*}
			where
			\[
			K_2=1+M_{1}\|P\|,\qquad K_3=C_2+2K_1,\qquad q=p+1=\frac{1}{1-\delta}.
			\]
			
			\textbf{Step 3}, Estimate \(\|C^{n}\|, n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}\).
			
			Let
		$
			r_n=1-\frac{1}{2}n^{-\frac{1}{q+1}}\ge \frac{1}{2},\  n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}
			$
		then \(-\log r_n\le 2(1-r_n)\), and hence
			\[
			(r_n)^{-n}=e^{-n\log r_n}\le e^{2n(1-r_n)}=e^{2n^{\frac{q}{q+1}}}.
			\]
			Clearly,
			\[
			(1-r_n)^q=n^{-\frac{q}{q+1}}.
			\]
			Therefore
			\[
			\|C^n\|\le e^{2n^{\frac{q}{q+1}}}K_2e^{K_3n^{\frac{q}{q+1}}}
			=K_2e^{(2+K_3)n^{\frac{q}{q+1}}}.
			\]
			Let
			\[
			\gamma=\frac{q}{q+1}=\frac{1}{2-\delta}\in(0,1),
			\]
			then
			\[
			\|C^n\|\le K_2e^{K_4n^\gamma},\qquad K_4=2+K_3.
			\]
			Similarly,
			\[
			\|D^n\|\le M_2e^{M_3n^\gamma}, n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}.
			\]
			
			
			Conversely, assume \(h_A(z_0)=0,\ z_0\in\mathbb D\). From \(\|C^n\|\le A_1e^{A_2n^\gamma},\ \gamma\in(0,1)\), we obtain \(r(C)\le1\). Take
			$
			x=F(z_0)Lu.
			$
			Then
			\[
			\begin{aligned}
				(I-z_0C)x&=(I-z_0L)x+z_0Px\\
				&=Lu+z_0\langle x,e_0\rangle Lu\\
				&=\bigl(1+z_0\langle x,e_0\rangle\bigr)Lu\\
				&=\bigl(1+z_0\langle F(z_0)Lu,e_0\rangle\bigr)Lu\\
				&=h_A(z_0)Lu\\
				&=0.
			\end{aligned}
			\]
			Since \(x\neq0\), and from \(r(C)\le1\) and \(|z_0|<1\), we know that \(I-z_0C\) is invertible. This contradicts \((I-z_0C)x=0\). Therefore \(h_A(z)\) is zero free on \(\mathbb D\). Similarly, \(h_B(z)\) is zero free on \(\mathbb D\).

body_md:
\label{tuilun22}
			Let \(T=\begin{pmatrix}A & T_{12}\\0 & B\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\langle T_{12}f_0,e_0\rangle=a\neq0\). Let \(A^{*},B\in B_{1}(O_{\delta})\). Let \(L,R\) be the standard left inverse and standard right inverse of \(A,B\), respectively, and there exist \(M\ge 1, \delta\in (0,1)\) such that
			\[
			\max\{\|A^n\|,\|B^n\|,\|L^n\|,\|R^n\|\}\le Me^{an^\delta}, n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}.
			\]
			Define
			\[
			C=L-LT_{12}f_0'\otimes e_0,\qquad D=R-f_0'\otimes R^*T_{12}^*e_0,\qquad f_0'=\frac{f_0}{a}.
			\]
			Then there exist constants \(A_{1}, A_{2}>0\) and \(\gamma\in (0,1)\) such that
			\[
			\|C^{n}\|,\|D^{n}\|\le A_{1}e^{A_{2}n^{\gamma}}, n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}
			\] if and only if
			\[
			h_A(z)=\langle(I-zL)^{-1}T_{12}f_0,e_0\rangle
			\]
			and
			\[
			h_B(z)=\langle T_{12}(I-zR)^{-1}f_0,e_0\rangle
			\]
			are zero free on \(\mathbb D\).

title: Proof
body_md:
It is easy to see that \(\langle T_{12}f_0',e_0\rangle=1\). Since \(a\neq0\) and \(f_0=a f_0'\), if \(h_A,h_B\) are zero free on \(\mathbb D\), then
			\[
			h_A'(z)=\langle(I-zL)^{-1}T_{12}f_0',e_0\rangle,\qquad
			h_B'(z)=\langle T_{12}(I-zR)^{-1}f_0',e_0\rangle

			are also zero free on \(\mathbb D\). Combining with \(\langle T_{12}f_0',e_0\rangle=1\), by Proposition \ref{mingttiiiB1}, we know that \(C,D\) satisfy subexponential growth.
			
			Conversely, if \(C,D\) satisfy subexponential growth, then by Proposition  \ref{mingttiiiB1}, \(a h_A(z),a h_B(z)\) are zero-free on \(\mathbb D\), and hence \(h_A(z),h_B(z)\) are zero free on \(\mathbb D\).

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{dingliB1}
			Let \(T=\begin{pmatrix}A & T_{12}\\0 & B\end{pmatrix}\) be a conjugate bi-geometric operator satisfying \(\sigma(T)=\mathbb{T}\) and \(\langle T_{12}f_0,e_0\rangle=a\neq0\). Let \(A^{*},B\in B_{1}(O_{t}), t\in (0,1)\). Let \(L,R\) be the standard left inverse and standard right inverse of \(A,B\), respectively, and there exist \(M\ge 1, \delta\in (0,1)\) such that

			\max\{\|A^n\|,\|B^n\|,\|L^n\|,\|R^n\|\}\le Me^{an^\delta}, n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}.
			\]
			If
			\[
			h_A(z)=\langle(I-zL)^{-1}T_{12}f_0,e_0\rangle,\qquad
			h_B(z)=\langle T_{12}(I-zR)^{-1}f_0,e_0\rangle

title: Example
body_md:
\label{tuilun1}
			Let
			\[
			T=\begin{pmatrix}S_\alpha & T_{12}\\0 & S_\beta^*\end{pmatrix}\in B(H^{2}(\alpha)\oplus H^{2}(\beta)),
			\]
			satisfy \(\sigma(T)=\mathbb{T}\) and \(\langle T_{12}f_0,e_0\rangle\ne 0\).
			If there exist \(\gamma \in(0,1),\) \(C_{1},C_{2}>0\) such that
			\[
			\max_{k\ge 0}\left\{\frac{\alpha_{k+n}}{\alpha_k},\frac{\alpha_k}{\alpha_{k+n}},\frac{\beta_{k+n}}{\beta_k},\frac{\beta_k}{\beta_{k+n}}\right\}\le C_{1}e^{C_{2}n^\delta},\ n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}
			\]
			and \(T_{12}f_0,\ T_{12}^*e_0\) are zero free on \(\mathbb D\), then \(T^{-1}\) is intransitive. In particular, \(T^{-1}\) possesses a nontrivial hyperinvariant subspace.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(L,R\) be the standard left inverse and standard right inverse of \(S_{\alpha},S_{\beta}^{*}\), respectively. Then
			\[
			h_{1}(z)=\langle (I-zL)^{-1}T_{12}f_{0},e_{0}\rangle =\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}z^{n}\langle T_{12}f_{0},L^{*n}e_{0}\rangle =\alpha_{0}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \langle T_{12}f_{0},e_{n}\rangle \dfrac{z^{n}}{\alpha_{n}}=\alpha_{0}(T_{12}f_{0})(z).
			\]
			Similarly,
			\[
			h_{2}(z)=\langle T_{12}(I-zR)^{-1}f_{0},e_{0}\rangle =\beta_{0}\overline{T_{12}^{*}e_{0}}(\overline{z}).
			\]
			Therefore, \(T_{12}f_{0},T_{12}^{*}e_{0}\) are zero free on \(\mathbb{D}\) if and only if \(h_{1},h_{2}\) are zero free on \(\mathbb{D}\). It is easy to see that
			\[
			\max_{k\ge 0}\left\{\frac{\alpha_{k+n}}{\alpha_k},\frac{\alpha_k}{\alpha_{k+n}},\frac{\beta_{k+n}}{\beta_k},\frac{\beta_k}{\beta_{k+n}}\right\}\le C_{1}e^{C_{2}n^\delta},n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}
			\]
			is equivalent to
			\[
			\|S_\alpha^n\|,\|L^n\|,\|(S_\beta^*)^n\|,\|R^n\|\le C_{1}e^{C_{2}n^\delta} ,\quad n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}.
			\]
			Hence, by Theorem \ref{dingliB1}, \(T^{-1}\) is intransitive and \(T^{-1}\) possesses a nontrivial hyperinvariant subspace.

label: juxianxing
title: Example
body_md:
\label{juxianxing}
				Let
			\[
			Te_k=w_{k}e_{k+1},\ w_{k}=e^{\frac{1}{\log(k+2)}}\quad k\ge0.
			\]
			Then
			\[
			\|T\|=\sup_{k\ge0} w_k = e^{\frac{1}{\log2}}<\infty.\qquad
			T^n e_k = e^{\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{\log(k+j+2)}} e_{k+n}, n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}.
			\]Hence,
			\[
			\|T^n\|=\sup_{k\ge0} e^{\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{\log(k+j+2)}}
			=e^{\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{\log(j+2)}}, n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}.
			\]
			Since
		$
			\frac{1}{\log(j+2)}\to 0,
			$
			we have
			$
			\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{\log(j+2)}\to 0.
			$
			Thus
			\[
			\|T^n\|^{\frac1n}=e^{\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{\log(j+2)}} \xrightarrow{n\to +\infty} 1.
			\]
			For $0\le j<n$, we have
			\[
			\frac{1}{\log(j+2)}\ge\frac{1}{\log(n+1)},
			\]
			so
			\[
			\|T^n\|\ge e^{\frac{n}{\log(n+1)}}.
			\]
			If $\|T^n\|\le M_{1} e^{M_2 n^\alpha}$ with $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and $M_{1},M_{2}>0$ are constants, then
			\[
			\frac{n}{\log(n+1)}\le \log M_{1} + M_2 n^\alpha,
			\]
			and hence
			\[
			\frac{n^{1-\alpha}}{\log(n+1)}\le \frac{\log M_{1}}{n^\alpha}+M_2.
			\]
		Since \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), it follows that
		\[
		\frac{n^{1-\alpha}}{\log(n+1)}\to+\infty \quad \text{as } n\to\infty,
		\]
		whereas the right-hand side is bounded, a contradiction. Therefore, it is impossible that \(\|T^n\|\le M_{1} e^{M_2 n^\alpha}, n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}\), i.e., $T$ does not have subexponential growth.
			
			Obviously, $T\in B_{1}(O_{\delta})$. Let $A=T(T^{*}T)^{-1}$, then $Ae_{k}=\dfrac{1}{w_{k}}e_{k+1}$. Let $p_{0}=1$ and $p_{n}=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}w_{j}=e^{\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{\log(j+2)}}$.
			Take $T_{12}=(e_{0}+e_{1})\otimes e_{0}$. Then clearly $\langle T_{12}e_{0},e_{0}\rangle =1$. Let
			\[
			e(\lambda)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\lambda^{n}A^{n}e_{0}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{\lambda^{n}}{p_{n}}e_{n},\qquad
			f(\lambda)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\lambda^{n}T^{n}e_{0}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\lambda^{n}p_{n}e_{n}.
			\]
			Let
			\[
			W=\begin{pmatrix}
				T&T_{12}\\
				0&T^{*}
			\end{pmatrix}.
			\]
			A direct computation shows that $T_{12}e(0)=e_{0}+e_{1}\ne f(0)$. Hence \(W\) neither has the bundle-preserving property nor satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{dingli00}. For such operators, we currently have no good method to solve the third problem of Halmos for this class of operators.

label: fangfafanli
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{fangfafanli}
			Suppose that
			\[
			\|T^n\|=e^{|n|\alpha_n},\quad n\in \mathbb{Z},
			\]
			where
			\[
			1-\frac{\log(\log(e+|n|))}{\log|n|}\le \alpha_n<1,\quad n\ge 0.
			\]
			If nonzero functions $\varphi,\psi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T})$ satisfy
			\[
			\sum_{n\in \mathbb{Z}}|\widehat{\varphi}(n)|\|T^{n}\|<+\infty,\quad
			\sum_{n\in \mathbb{Z}}|\widehat{\psi}(n)|\|T^{n}\|<+\infty,
			\]
			then $\varphi\psi\not \equiv 0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We argue by contradiction. Suppose that \(\varphi\psi\equiv 0\).
			
			From
			\[
			1>\alpha_k\ge 1-\frac{\log(\log(e+|k|))}{\log|k|},
			\]
			it is clear that $\alpha_k\to1$. Moreover,
			\[
			|k|^{\alpha_k}\ge \frac{|k|}{|k|^{\frac{\log(\log(e+|k|))}{\log|k|}}}=\dfrac{|k|}{\log(e+|k|)}.
			\]
			Let
			\[
			A=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|a_k|\|T^k\|<+\infty,
			\]
			where \(a_k\) are the Fourier coefficients of \(\varphi\). Then
			\[
			|a_k|\|T^k\|\le A
			\implies
			|a_k|\le \frac{A}{\|T^k\|}
			=A e^{-|k|^{\alpha_k}}
			\le A e^{-|k|\frac{1}{\log(e+|k|)}}.
			\]
			Let
			\[
			w(x)=\frac{1}{\log(e+|x|)},\ x\in \mathbb{R},
			\]
			then
			\[
			|\widehat{\varphi}(k)|= |a_k|\le A e^{-|k|w(k)},\quad k\in\mathbb Z.
			\]
			For \(w(x)=\frac{1}{\log(e+|x|)}\), obviously \(w\) is a radial function,
			\[
			\lim_{|x|\to\infty}w(x)=0,
			\]and $w \text{ is radially strictly decreasing}.$
			Since for \(m\ge3\),
			\[
			\log(e+m)\le \log m^2=2\log m,
			\]
			we have
			\[
			\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}\frac{w(m)}{m}
			=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{m\log(e+|m|)}
			=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{m\log(e+m)}
			\ge \sum_{m=3}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2m\log m}
			=+\infty.
			\]
		
			
			Since \(\psi\not\equiv 0\) and \(\psi\) is continuous, there exists a nonempty open set \(U\subset\mathbb T\) on which \(\psi\) does not vanish. From \(\varphi\psi\equiv 0\) we obtain \(\varphi\equiv 0\) on \(U\). Hence we conclude that \(\varphi\equiv0\) by Lemma \ref{ingatem}, a contradiction.

title: Proposition
body_md: Let \(T=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&B\end{pmatrix}\) be an essentially unitary operator, and let \(A^{*},B\in B_1(O_{\delta})\). Then \(A,B\) are essentially unitary operators and \(C\) is compact.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since \(A^*,B\in B_1(O_\delta)\), the operators \(A,B,A^*,B^*\) are all Fredholm. Hence \[\pi(A),\pi(B),\pi(A^*),\pi(B^*)\] are invertible. From \(\pi(T^*)\pi(T)=\pi(T)\pi(T^*)=I\), it follows that \(\pi(C^*)\pi(C)=0\). Thus \(\pi(C)=0\), i.e., \(C\) is compact. Meanwhile,
	\[
	\pi(A^*)\pi(A)=\pi(A)\pi(A^*)=I,\qquad
	\pi(B)\pi(B^*)=\pi(B^*)\pi(B)=I.
	\]
	Therefore \(A,B\) are both essentially unitary. Moreover, it follows that \(A^{*},B\in B_{1}(\mathbb{D})\).

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{5.2.2.2}
	The following two statements are equivalent:
	
	(1) If \(T\) is an essentially unitary invertible operator and has a nontrivial invariant subspace, then \(T^{-1}\) is intransitive.
	
	(2) If $T$
	is a conjugate bi-geometric operator, invertible, and essentially unitary, then \(T^{-1}\) is intransitive.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\((1)\Rightarrow(2)\) obviously.
	
	\((2)\Rightarrow(1)\): Suppose \(T\) is essentially unitary invertible and has an invariant subspace. Then we can write
	\[
	T=\begin{pmatrix}A&T_{12}\\0&B\end{pmatrix}.
	\]
 If \(A^{*},B \not \in B_1(O_{\delta})\), then by Theorem \ref{thm:1.1}, \(T^{-1}\) is intransitive;
	If \(A^{*},B\in B_1(O_{\delta})\), then \(T^{-1}\) is intransitive by (2).

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{5.3.3.3}
	Let \(T\) be an essentially unitary operator that is invertible and intransitive. If \(\sigma(T)\not\subset\mathbb{T}\), then \(T^{-1}\) is intransitive.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If \(\sigma(T)\not\subset\mathbb{T}\), then there exists \(\lambda\in\sigma(T)\) with \(\lambda\notin\mathbb{T}\). Since \(T\) is essentially unitary, we have \(\sigma_{e}(T)\subset\mathbb{T}\).
	
	Thus \(\lambda\in\rho_F(T)\). If \(\lambda\in\mathbb{D}\), then since \(T\) is invertible, \(\operatorname{ind}T=0\), and by the continuity of the index, we obtain
	$
	\operatorname{ind}(T-\lambda I)=0.
	$
	And \(T-\lambda I\) is not invertible, so \(\ker(T-\lambda I)\neq\{0\}\), and hence \(T^{-1}\) is intransitive.
	
	If \(\lambda\in\mathbb{D}^c\), take \(|\mu|>\|T\|\). Then \(\operatorname{ind}(T-\mu I)=0\), so \(\operatorname{ind}(T-\lambda I)=0\). Similarly, \(T^{-1}\) is intransitive.
	
	If \(\sigma(T)\not\subset\mathbb{T}\), it follows that every invariant subspace of \(T\) is also an invariant subspace of \(T^{-1}\). Hence \(T^{-1}\) is intransitive.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{5.4.4.4}
Consequently, it follows from Propositions \ref{5.2.2.2} and \ref{5.3.3.3} that, in the study of Halmos's third problem for essentially unitary operators, it suffices to consider the case in which \(T\) is a conjugate bi-geometric operator that is essentially unitary and satisfies \(\sigma(T)=\mathbb{T}\).

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(M = \sup_{N \geq 0} \|A_N(K)\|\) and take a polynomial \(p \in H^2\) of degree at most \(m\). Since \((S^*)^r p = 0\) for \(r > m\), it follows that \(A_N(K)p = \sum_{r=0}^m (S^*)^{r+1} K (S^*)^r p\). Let
 	\[
 	X(p) = \lim_{N} A_N(K)p = \sum_{r=0}^m (S^*)^{r+1} K (S^*)^r p.
 	\]
 	Consequently, \(\|X(p)\| \leq M\|p\|\). Hence $X\in B(H^{2})$. Now, for any \(f \in H^2\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a polynomial \(p\) such that \(\|f - p\| < \frac{\varepsilon}{M}\), and
 	\[
 	\|A_N(K)p - X(p)\| \to 0.
 	\]
 	Therefore, there exists \(N_1 > 0\) such that for all \(N > N_1\), we have \(\|A_N(K)p - Xp\| \leq \varepsilon\), and hence \[\|A_N(K)f - Xf\| \leq \|A_N(K)(f-p) + A_N(K)p - Xp + X(f-p)\| \leq 3\varepsilon,\] so \(A_N(K) \xrightarrow{SOT} X\). Therefore,
 	\begin{align*}
 		x_{0,n-1} &= \langle X e_{n-1}, e_0 \rangle \\
 		&= \lim_{N \to \infty} \langle A_N(K) e_{n-1}, e_0 \rangle \\
 		&= \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} \langle (S^*)^{r+1} K e_{n-1-r}, e_0 \rangle \\
 		&= \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} \langle K e_{n-1-r}, e_{1+r} \rangle \\
 		& = \sum_{r=1}^{n} k_{r, n-r}.
 	\end{align*}
 	It follows that \(A_N(K) - S^* A_N(K) S^* = S^* K - (S^*)^{N+2} K (S^*)^{N+1}\), let \(N \to +\infty\), we get \(X - S^* X S^* = S^* K\). Let \(D = S X - X S^* - K\), we have \(S^* D = 0\), and
 	\[
 	\langle D e_n, e_0 \rangle = \langle (S X - X S^*) e_n, e_0) \rangle - \langle K e_n, e_0 \rangle = -x_{0, n-1} - k_{0, n} = -\sum_{j=0}^n k_{j, n-j} = 0,

 	and \(\langle D e_0, e_0 \rangle = -k_{0,0} = 0\), so \(ran D \subset \bigvee \{e_n : n \geq 1\}\), combined with \(S^* D = 0\), so \(D = 0\), hence \(S X - X S^* = K\). Let \(P_n = I - S^n (S^*)^n\), since \(S^n (S^*)^n e_j = \begin{cases} 0, & j < n \\ e_j, & j \geq n \end{cases}\), therefore \(ran P_n = \bigvee \{e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}\}\), so \(P_n K\) is a finite rank operator and
 	\[
 	\|K - P_n K\| = \|S^n (S^*)^n K\| = \|(S^*)^n K\| \xrightarrow{n\to \infty} 0,
 	\]
 	i.e., \(K = \lim_{n \to \infty} P_n K\), hence \(K \in K(H^2)\), so \(K \in ran \tau_{S, S^*} \cap K(H^2)\).
 	
 	Since \(\tilde{T}\) has the bundle-preserving property, \((T_{12} - K)e_n = \alpha^n e_n\), and \(|\alpha| < 1,\ n\in \mathbb{N}_{0}\), since \(T_{12} - K \in K(H^2)\), so \(T_{12}=T_{12}-K+K \in K(H^2)\). Therefore, \(T\) is an essentially unitary operator. Together with Corollary \ref{collo3.6}, it implies that \(T^{-1}\) is intransitive.

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let
 	\[
 	T=\begin{pmatrix}
 		A & T_{12}\\
 		0 & B
 	\end{pmatrix}\in B(\mathcal{H}_{1}\oplus \mathcal{H}_{2}),
 	\]
 	and suppose that $T^{-1}$ is intransitive. Let
 	\[
 	\tilde{T}=\begin{pmatrix}
 		\tilde{A} & \tilde{A}_{12}\\
 		0 & \tilde{B}
 	\end{pmatrix}\in B(\tilde{\mathcal{H}}_{1}\oplus \tilde{\mathcal{H}_{2}}),
 	\]
 	where $A^{*},\tilde{A}^{*},B,\tilde{B}\in B_{1}(O_{\delta})$.
 	Denote by $S$ and $\tilde{S}$ the induced operators of $T$ and $\tilde{T}$, respectively.
 	Let $\gamma(w)$ be a section spanning $\ker(S-w)$, and $\delta(w)$ a section spanning $\ker(S^{*}-w)$.
 	If the following conditions hold:
 	\begin{enumerate}
 		\item $\mathcal{K}_{A^{*}}(w)=\mathcal{K}_{\tilde{A}^{*}}(w)$.
 		
 		\item $\mathcal{K}_{B}(w)=\mathcal{K}_{\tilde{B}}(w)$.
 		
 		\item
 		$
 		\dfrac{\bigl|\langle\gamma(w_{1}),T_{12}\delta(\overline{w}_{2})\rangle\bigr|}
 		{\|\gamma(w_{1})\|\,\|\delta(\overline{w}_{2})\|}
 		=
 		\dfrac{\bigl|\langle\tilde{\gamma}(w_{1}),\tilde{A}_{12}\tilde{\delta}(\overline{w}_{2})\rangle\bigr|}
 		{\|\tilde{\gamma}(w_{1})\|\,\|\tilde{\delta}(\overline{w}_{2})\|},
 		$
 		for all $w,w_{1},w_{2}\in O_{\delta}$.
 	\end{enumerate}
 	then $\tilde{T}$ is invertible and $\tilde{T}^{-1}$ is intransitive.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
From conditions (1) and (2), we obtain
 	\[
 	\|P_{2}(w)SP_{2}(w)\|=\|\tilde{P}_{2}(w)\tilde{S}\tilde{P}_{2}(w)\|,\quad
 	\|Q_{2}(w)SQ_{2}(w)\|=\|\tilde{Q}_{2}(w)\tilde{S}\tilde{Q}_{2}(w)\|.
 	\]
 	Where $P_{i}(w)$ denotes the orthogonal projection onto $\ker(S-w)^{i}$ for $i=1,2$, and $Q_{j}(w)$ denotes the orthogonal projection onto $\ker(S-w)^{*j}$ for $j=1,2$. Since
 	\[
 	P_{2}(w)(S-w)P_{2}(w)
 	=(S-w)\big|_{\ker(S-w)^{2}}
 	=(S_{1}-w)\big|_{\ker(S_{1}-w)^{2}}
 	=\begin{pmatrix}
 		0 & h_{1}(w)\\
 		0 & 0
 	\end{pmatrix},
 	\]
 	we have
 	\[
 	P_{2}(w)SP_{2}(w)=\begin{pmatrix}
 		w & h_{1}(w)\\
 		0 & w
 	\end{pmatrix}.
 	\]
 	Similarly,
 	\[
 	\tilde{P}_{2}(w)\tilde{S}\tilde{P}_{2}(w)=\begin{pmatrix}
 		w & \tilde{h}_{1}(w)\\
 		0 & w
 	\end{pmatrix}.
 	\]
 	By (1), $h_{1}(w)=\tilde{h}_{1}(w)$, hence $S_{1}\sim_{u}\tilde{S}_{1}$.
 	
 	Similarly, from condition (2), we obtain $S_{2}^{*}\sim_{u}\tilde{S}_{2}^{*}$, so $S_{2}\sim_{u}\tilde{S}_{2}$.
 	Together with condition (3) and Remark \ref{rem:2.7}, we get $S\sim_{u}\tilde{S}$.
 	Since $S,\tilde{S}\in B_{1,1}(\Omega)$, it follows from Lemma \ref{4.1} that there exists a unitary operator
 	\[
 	U=\begin{pmatrix}
 		U_{1} & U_{12}\\
 		0 & U_{2}
 	\end{pmatrix}
 	\]such that $US=\tilde{S}U$.
 	
 From the proof of Lemma \ref{4.1}, it follows that $U^{-1}$ is also an upper triangular matrix. Moreover, since $U$ is unitary, we have $U^* = U^{-1}$. Consequently, $U$ is a diagonal operator, i.e.\[
 	U=\begin{pmatrix}
 	U_{1} & 0\\
 	0 & U_{2}
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \]
 The identity $US=\tilde{S}U$ yields
 	\[
 	\begin{cases}
 		U_{1}A^{*}=\tilde{A}^{*}U_{1}\\[4pt]
 		U_{2}B^{*}=\tilde{B}^{*}U_{2}\\[4pt]
 		U_{1}T_{12}=\tilde{A}_{12}U_{2}
 	\end{cases}.
 	\]
 	Therefore, we have
 	\[
 	U_{1}A=\tilde{A}U_{1},\quad U_{2}B=\tilde{B}U_{2}.
 	\]
 	
 Consequently,
 	\[
 	\begin{pmatrix}
 		U_{1} & 0\\
 		0 & U_{2}
 	\end{pmatrix}
 	\begin{pmatrix}
 		A & T_{12}\\
 		0 & B
 	\end{pmatrix}
 	=
 	\begin{pmatrix}
 		U_{1}A & U_{1}T_{12}\\
 		0 & U_{2}B
 	\end{pmatrix}
 	=
 	\begin{pmatrix}
 		\tilde{A} & \tilde{A}_{12}\\
 		0 & \tilde{B}
 	\end{pmatrix}
 	\begin{pmatrix}
 		U_{1} & 0\\
 		0 & U_{2}
 	\end{pmatrix}.
 	\]
 	Thus $T\sim_{u}\tilde{T}$, it implies that $\tilde{T}^{-1}$ is intransitive.
